abandon: The board already measured what m03 predicts and found the opposite. m03 says misreadings happen because the cued base does not copy the problem's givens word for word near the start of its answer, so it later reads them from its own paraphrase. A verbatim restatement in the early text shows up as high problem dependence: log p(token | problem) - log p(token | no problem), averaged over the first 1,000 tokens. This is large on copied tokens. About 80 copied tokens at a few nats each would move the 1,000-token mean by about 0.2 nats, more than the gaps between labels. result-f3d708 computed this quantity for all 2,000 stored cued-base samples. (1) Misread samples are not the least problem-dependent: "Predictions P1 and P3 refuted: misread samples do not have the lowest value (0.132 nats per token; slip 0.094, wrong plan 0.154)." So misread answers depend on the problem text more than slip answers do, not less. (2) Right and wrong siblings of the same problem do not differ: the statistic "ranks the right sample above the wrong one of the same problem in 53.1 % of pairs [46.8, 58.9]; chance is 50." Under m03, right siblings should carry the restatement that wrong siblings lack. knowledge-16c62a lists this test among the closed routes: "problem dependence log p(tok|problem) - log p(tok|no problem) 0.531 [0.468, 0.589] (result-f3d708)". The early setup in result-c495fe ("a misreading starts before its sentence") is still real, but the in-context-copy cause m03 gives for it is contradicted. Also, the facts.json r7-m05 numbers show that deleting the problem raises misread and wrong-plan steps alike (0.686 vs 0.688), which does not single out misreadings as a failure to read the givens. m03's proposed coverage statistic would mostly re-measure what f3d708 already found to be null.
